The newly hatched Pharaonic mussel emerges with a shell height of only 0.009 centimeters [Lb = 0.009 centimeters], a diminutive size measured from the umbo to the ventral margin that places it among the smallest recorded mytilid larvae. This initial dimension reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the early veliger, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during its first days of pelagic development. In laboratory cultures maintained at a stable 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the period between egg hatching and the onset of the planktotrophic stage is remarkably brief, with individuals beginning to feed exogenously after just 1.1 days [ab = 1.1 days], a value derived from studies on the congener Brachidontes solisianus. The rapid transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition is critical for larval survival in the variable thermal regimes of the Mediterranean and Red Sea, where this invasive species has become established.

Following the trochophore stage, the developing veliger undergoes significant shell growth before reaching metamorphic competence. At a water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the time elapsed since birth at which the larva attains the pediveliger stage and is competent to settle is approximately 24 days since birth , a figure documented for Brachidontes solisianus that appears applicable to B. pharaonis given their phylogenetic proximity. The shell height at this metamorphic event is 0.0273 centimeters , marking the transition from a planktonic to a benthic existence. This morphological transformation involves the reabsorption of the velum and the development of functional gills, allowing the newly settled spat to commence filter-feeding on phytoplankton. The precise timing of settlement is ecologically consequential, as it determines the extent of advection away from parental populations and influences subsequent recruitment success on hard substrates such as rocky shores and artificial structures.

After settlement, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a phase of rapid somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of reproductive maturity. Under thermal conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], puberty, defined as the onset of gametogenesis and the development of functional gonads, is reached approximately 182 days after birth [tp = approximately 182 days after birth]. At this stage, the individual achieves a wet weight at puberty of 0.084 grams [Wwp = 0.084 grams] and a corresponding shell height of 0.75 centimeters [Lp = 0.75 centimeters], measured from the umbo to the ventral margin. The congruence between the mass and length thresholds for maturity suggests a deterministic relationship between size and sexual development, a pattern observed in many iteroparous bivalves. The relatively fast maturation time of about six months, compared to other mytilids such as Mytilus galloprovincialis, may partially explain the invasive success of B. pharaonis in oligotrophic environments where rapid establishment is advantageous.

At full adulthood, the maximum shell height recorded for Brachidontes pharaonis asymptotically approaches 3.8 centimeters [Li = 3.8 centimeters], a dimension that represents the upper bound of somatic growth under optimal conditions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual is 1.5456 grams [Wwi = 1.5456 grams], a value that integrates both somatic tissue and gonadal mass during the reproductive season. The lifespan of this species under natural conditions, based on growth-ring analysis and mark-recapture studies conducted at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], extends to approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years], with the oldest recorded individuals exhibiting signs of gonadal senescence and reduced byssal attachment. Compared to congeneric species inhabiting similar thermal regimes, this longevity is intermediate, reflecting a trade-off between early reproductive output and sustained physiological performance over multiple spawning seasons.

Reproductive output in Brachidontes pharaonis is substantial and tightly coupled to the thermal environment. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females produce a maximum of approximately 1,208 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,208 eggs per day], a reproductive rate that translates into an annual fecundity that can exceed 440,000 eggs per individual under favorable conditions. This prodigious spawning capacity is facilitated by continuous gametogenesis during the warm season, with multiple spawning events triggered by temperature fluctuations and phytoplankton blooms. The 0.009-centimeter shell height at birth (0.009 centimeters) [Lb = 0.009 centimeters] underscores the vast size disparity between the microscopic propagule and the 1.5456-gram adult (1.5456 grams) [Wwi = 1.5456 grams], representing a mass increase of over four orders of magnitude across the life cycle. Such high fecundity, combined with the short generation time of approximately six months to puberty (approximately 182 days after birth) [tp = approximately 182 days after birth], confers a demographic advantage that has facilitated the rapid spread of this Lessepsian migrant throughout the eastern Mediterranean basin at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
